claims.text: Dynamic mechanical behavior in the proposed fcc high-entropy alloys arises primarily from a mechanically induced, continuous nanoscale fcc-to-hcp transformation.
Stacking-fault networks generate incipient hcp regions during loading.
Localized hcp regions act as transient barriers to dislocation motion.
The transformation-induced barriers increase strain hardening and strength without severely reducing ductility.
The Cantor alloy is equiatomic, and it and its CrCoNi derivative exhibit exceptional damage tolerance that improves at cryogenic temperatures.
CrCoNi and the Cantor alloy can serve as equiatomic, single-phase fcc initial states for the proposed test.
The proposed CrCoNi or Cantor initial state is prone to low-stacking-fault-energy defects.
Heat treatment, microstructural modification, or alloying can suppress stacking-fault formation and the associated fcc-to-hcp transformation.
Under suitable dynamic loading conditions, deformation kinetics permit stacking-fault nucleation followed by an fcc-to-hcp transformation.
Low stacking-fault energy in the fcc phase facilitates formation of stacking-fault networks under load.
Stacking-fault networks initiate a partial in situ transformation from fcc to hcp.
The hcp structure is intrinsically stronger but more brittle than the parent fcc phase.
Coexistence of a ductile matrix and stronger hcp regions can produce a strength-ductility combination.
Transformation-induced barriers increase strain hardening, delay necking, and thereby preserve ductility while increasing strength.
Relative to a transformation-suppressed baseline, the transforming alloy will have higher yield strength and greater strain-hardening capacity.
The transforming alloy will maintain overall ductility despite the formation of locally brittle hcp regions.
The mechanism should operate only when the fcc phase has sufficiently low stacking-fault energy and transformation kinetics are active.
High stacking-fault energy, very low strain rates, or extreme microstructural stabilization should suppress the proposed mechanism.
Deformation twinning may contribute to the response and has not been fully decoupled from the proposed phase-transformation mechanism.
The beneficial hcp-phase fraction before ductility is compromised is not known precisely.
